item.title: A1 · Can People Still Afford Rent? Then vs Now
item.description: 1. The headline average has barely moved. According to the Federal Statistical Office's microcensus housing survey, the average tenant household spent twenty-seven point nine percent of its net income on rent, excluding heating, in twenty twenty-two. In two thousand and six the figure was about twenty-seven percent, and the German Institute for Economic Research, DIW Berlin, finds the average roughly flat since about two thousand and five. Beneath that average, about one in six tenant households, some three point one million, paid forty percent or more of their income, and about one in twelve paid at least half. One caution: the statistical office says the twenty twenty-two survey was redesigned, so comparisons with earlier years are possible only to a very limited extent. 2. Over the longer run, rent did take a bigger bite. The statistical office's own retrospective, quoted by the Bundestag's research service, reported that in nineteen sixty more than half of tenant households paid less than ten percent of their income in rent. By nineteen ninety-eight the average had reached twenty-four and a half percent, roughly double the level of fifty years earlier. The statistical office put much of that rise down to larger, better-equipped flats and smaller households. 3. The gap between poorer and richer tenants is steep. In the twenty twenty-two microcensus, households with less than one thousand five hundred euros a month paid forty-four point six percent of their income in rent, while households with four thousand euros or more paid fifteen point nine percent. Low-income households of four or more people paid fifty-eight percent. 4. For the poorest, the burden rose substantially over three decades. Kholodilin and Baake at DIW Berlin, using the Socio-Economic Panel, find that the poorest fifth of tenant households went from about twenty-four percent of income in nineteen ninety to about thirty-six percent in twenty twenty-one, while the richest fifth paid about twenty-one percent. The economists Dustmann, Fitzenberger and Zimmermann, writing in The Economic Journal, find a similar pattern for the bottom fifth of all households: from twenty-seven to thirty-nine percent between nineteen ninety-three and twenty thirteen, with most of the rise coming before about two thousand and eight. 5. Sitting tenants and people who move are in two different markets. Eurostat's price index for existing rents in Germany rose about twenty-six percent between twenty ten and twenty twenty-five, while pay per employee rose about sixty-two percent. But the Federal Institute for Building, Urban Affairs and Spatial Development reports that advertised rents in large cities nearly doubled over the same period, from seven euros forty to fourteen euros per square metre. In twenty twenty-five, advertised rents nationwide were about forty-three percent above the average rent in existing contracts, and in Munich they reached about twenty-one euros. The institute itself cautions that online listings under-represent cheaper flats. 6. That gap shows up in household budgets too, if less dramatically. In the twenty twenty-two microcensus, tenants who moved in from twenty nineteen onwards paid twenty-nine point six percent of their income, against twenty-six point nine percent for those whose contracts began before nineteen ninety-nine. Dustmann and his co-authors find that rent increases are far higher for movers than for stayers, and that the lowest income group moves most often. 7. Place matters. In twenty twenty-two, tenants in large cities paid on average twenty-nine percent of their income, against twenty-six percent in small towns and rural municipalities. Among the federal states, the range ran from Saxony at about twenty-three percent to Bremen at nearly thirty-one. 8. How Germany compares with Europe depends on whom you count. Eurostat's twenty twenty-five data show that thirty-five percent of people at risk of poverty in Germany spend more than forty percent of their disposable income on housing, above the European Union average of about twenty-nine percent. But among tenants paying market rents, Germany's rate of thirteen point two percent is below the European average of eighteen point six. 9. Housing benefit softens the edges, but not everywhere. According to the Federal Statistical Office, the twenty twenty-three Wohngeld Plus reform raised the number of households receiving housing benefit by eighty percent, to almost one point two million by the end of that year. Yet the Cologne-based German Economic Institute notes that in twenty twenty-four fewer than one percent of those households lived in the most expensive rent level, which includes Munich. 10. The safety net of social housing has shrunk while high burdens spread. Kholodilin and Baake report that the number of social housing units fell from about four million in the late nineteen eighties to about one million at the end of twenty twenty-two. Since two thousand and two, the share of tenant households paying more than forty percent of their income has exceeded the share living in social housing, and by twenty twenty-one it was almost twice as high.
